candidates.teaser: Every banana you've ever eaten was slightly radioactive — and nobody told you.
candidates.video_title: Every Banana You've Eaten Is Radioactive
candidates.video_description: Bananas contain potassium-40, a naturally radioactive isotope. While a single banana won't harm you, the radiation is real and measurable — and it's even used as an informal unit of measurement by scientists.
candidates.script: Every banana you've ever eaten was radioactive. Not metaphorically — literally. Bananas contain potassium-40, a naturally occurring radioactive isotope. Scientists actually invented an unofficial unit called the 'Banana Equivalent Dose' to compare radiation levels. A dental X-ray? About 50 bananas. A flight from New York to London? Roughly 400 bananas. You've been eating tiny doses of radiation your entire life. So — how many bananas is too many?

candidates.topic: Oxford University older than the Aztec Empire
candidates.teaser: One of the world's greatest empires rose and fell — and Oxford University was already ancient by then.
candidates.video_title: Oxford Is Older Than the Entire Aztec Empire
candidates.video_description: Oxford University began teaching as early as 1096 AD. The Aztec Empire wasn't founded until 1428 — meaning Oxford was already over 300 years old when the Aztecs built Tenochtitlan. History has a strange sense of scale.
candidates.script: Oxford University was already 300 years old before the Aztec Empire even existed. Oxford began teaching in 1096. The Aztecs didn't found their empire until 1428. By the time Aztec warriors were building Tenochtitlan, Oxford students had already graduated for over three centuries. The empire that seemed eternal? Gone by 1521. Oxford? Still running. Which one do you think history got right?

candidates.topic: Mantis shrimp can see colors humans cannot
candidates.teaser: There's a creature on Earth that sees an entire universe of color you will never be able to imagine.
candidates.video_title: This Animal Sees Colors You Can't Even Imagine
candidates.video_description: Humans see the world through 3 color receptors. The mantis shrimp has 16 — giving it access to colors completely outside human perception, including ultraviolet and infrared. Its punch is also fast enough to boil water on impact.
candidates.script: There's a creature that sees colors your brain is physically incapable of processing. The mantis shrimp has 16 types of color receptors. Humans have 3. It perceives ultraviolet light, infrared, and hues that have no name in any human language because no human has ever seen them. It also punches hard enough to shatter aquarium glass. It's been sharing our planet for 400 million years — seeing a world completely invisible to us.

candidates.topic: Stomach acid strong enough to dissolve metal
candidates.teaser: Inside your body right now, there's an acid powerful enough to dissolve a razor blade.
candidates.video_title: Your Stomach Acid Can Dissolve a Razor Blade
candidates.video_description: Human stomach acid (hydrochloric acid) has a pH between 1.5 and 3.5 — corrosive enough to dissolve metal. The only reason it doesn't destroy your stomach is a protective mucus lining that regenerates every two weeks.
candidates.script: Right now, inside your stomach, there's an acid strong enough to dissolve a razor blade. Hydrochloric acid — with a pH as low as 1.5 — can corrode certain metals on contact. The only thing standing between that acid and your own body is a thin layer of mucus. That mucus completely replaces itself every two weeks. If it fails even slightly, the acid starts digesting you from the inside. It's already happened to millions of people — they call it an ulcer.

candidates.topic: The Great Wall of China is not visible from space
candidates.teaser: One of the most repeated facts you learned in school is completely false — and astronauts proved it.
candidates.video_title: Astronauts Debunked This 'Fact' You Learned in School
candidates.video_description: Contrary to popular belief, the Great Wall of China cannot be seen from space with the naked eye. Chinese astronaut Yang Liwei confirmed this after his 2003 mission. The wall is simply too narrow — it's like trying to spot a single human hair from two miles away.
candidates.script: The Great Wall of China is visible from space — except it's completely false, and a Chinese astronaut proved it. Yang Liwei orbited Earth in 2003 specifically looking for it. He saw nothing. The wall is only about 5 meters wide. Spotting it from orbit would be like seeing a single human hair from two miles away. You were taught this 'fact' in school, it's in encyclopedias — and none of it is real. What else did they get wrong?
